articles.title: Verstappen saca el dedo a Hamilton y casi chocan a lo 2021
articles.standfirst: Max creyó que Hamilton le había arruinado una vuelta y se intentó tomar venganza de forma un tanto pendenciera
articles.summary: Max creyó que Hamilton le había arruinado una vuelta y se intentó tomar venganza de forma un tanto pendenciera
articles.body: En cierto que las velocidades no son las mismas que otros años y que se nota que el motor térmico no se basta del todo para ver aquellas puntas de más de 350 km/h en Monza. Piastri marcó 337 km/h como máxima en los Libres 3 del GP de Italia. Pero sigue siendo un circuito al límite, bajando marcha en la doble de Lesmo, donde entra el freno motor y controlar el coche es muy complicado, como en la reducción de la Variante Ascari, con sus tres pianos. Checo tuvo problemas al salir de Lesmo, levantó una nube de polvo y arruinó la vuelta buena de Hamilton en esos libres 3, aunque luego dio otras que le sirvió para ser segundo. Y Max llegaba por detrás y creyó que el que le había fastidiado era Lewis... Se quejó por la radio diciendo: "Otra vez el Ferrari, Dios mío". Pero ahí no acabó la cosa. Unos giros después, cuando ya no estaban en vuelta rápida, Verstappen y Hamilton llegaron emparejado en la curva 1, la Primera Variante, donde se intentó colar por dentro, echando al británico. Y fue cuando casi se tocan. El pasaje de 2021, cuando el de Red Bull quedó montado sobre el halo y con la rueda tocando el casco amarillo de Lewis, regresó de inmediato a la mente de los aficionados. Los comisarios tomaron nota y ambos debieron pasar por comisarios para dar explicaciones, pero era algo completamente innecesario y un tanto pendenciero, por parte del holandés, al que le hirvió la sangre como en tiempos no tan lejanos.

images.caption: Max y Hamilton, en el momento de su pique en los Libres 3. F1TV

articles.title: Kimi Antonelli becomes first Italian to lead F1 championship into Monza GP since 1953, carries Italy’s hopes and revives a dream last seen with Alberto Ascari
articles.summary: Racing News: For decades, Italian Formula 1 fans have dreamed of seeing one of their own arrive at Monza with the world championship within reach. In 2026, that wa.
articles.body: For decades, Italian Formula 1 fans have dreamed of seeing one of their own arrive at Monza with the world championship within reach. In 2026, that wait finally ended. Andrea Kimi Antonelli heads into the Italian Grand Prix as the Formula 1 World Championship leader, becoming the first Italian driver in 73 years to occupy the top spot in the standings ahead of his home race. The last to do it was Ferrari great Alberto Ascari in 1953.At just 20, Antonelli has already turned what was supposed to be a promising young career into one of the defining stories of the 2026 F1 season. Driving for Mercedes, the Bologna-born driver has won six Grands Prix and leads the championship with 242 points, 59 clear of his teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, both on 183.73 years after Ascari, Italy has its championship leaderThe name Alberto Ascari remains synonymous with Italian Formula 1 greatness. Driving for Ferrari, Ascari won consecutive world championships in 1952 and 1953. In 1953, he arrived at the Italian Grand Prix leading the Drivers' Championship, a feat no Italian had repeated at their home race until Antonelli's breakthrough this year.The parallel is particularly striking because Ascari's 1953 season ended with him finishing the championship as world champion, despite retiring from the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.Now, 73 years later, another Italian has arrived at Monza carrying the country's championship hopes. The difference is that Antonelli is doing it in a Mercedes rather than a Ferrari.The 'Kimmy effect' takes over ItalyAntonelli's rise has sparked a new wave of enthusiasm around Italian motorsport. His emergence gives the country's fans something they have rarely had in the modern F1 era: an Italian driver capable of competing for the biggest prize in the sport.And he has done it quickly. After making his F1 debut with Mercedes in 2025 as Lewis Hamilton's replacement, Antonelli has exploded into title contention in his second season. His 2026 campaign already includes six victories and six pole positions from 12 Grands Prix.His success has also created an unusual dynamic at Monza. The Italian Grand Prix traditionally revolves around Ferrari and its passionate Tifosi. This year, however, the home crowd has another driver to cheer for, even though he is wearing Mercedes colours. That makes Antonelli's story different from those of previous Italian favourites. He does not need to drive a Ferrari to become a national sporting icon.From Hamilton's replacement to championship leaderThe expectations surrounding Antonelli were enormous from the moment Mercedes promoted him.He was only 18 when the team handed him Hamilton's seat following the seven-time world champion's move to Ferrari. Mercedes had effectively placed one of the sport's biggest responsibilities on the shoulders of a teenager.Antonelli responded with three podiums and 150 points in his rookie season. The second year has been a completely different story. He has established himself as the driver to beat, winning six races and building a substantial championship advantage. The irony is difficult to ignore: Hamilton, the man Antonelli replaced at Mercedes, is now one of his closest championship rivals, and is driving for Ferrari.Monza presents a very different challengeAntonelli's historic weekend will not be straightforward. A power-unit change means the championship leader is set to start the Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid, turning what could have been a straightforward homecoming into a recovery mission.Rather than allowing the penalty to overwhelm him, Antonelli has said it takes some pressure away and gives him the chance to enjoy his home race. That could make Sunday's contest even more compelling. The championship leader will have to fight his way through the field at one of the fastest circuits on the calendar while Ferrari drivers Hamilton and Charles Leclerc chase glory in front of their home fans.Mercedes teammate Russell, meanwhile, has already shown strong pace at Monza, topping Friday's second practice session and cutting into the attention surrounding Antonelli.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Sainz brilla y pasa a la Q2, contra pronóstico
articles.standfirst: Gran Q1 de Carlos, que dejó fuera a Tsunoda y Albon, con coches iguales o superiores y saldrá 14º en parrilla
articles.summary: Gran Q1 de Carlos, que dejó fuera a Tsunoda y Albon, con coches iguales o superiores y saldrá 14º en parrilla
articles.body: Uno de los detalles del sábado en el GP de Italia lo ha dejado Carlos Sainz, que con tres vueltas con tres juegos nuevos del compuesto blando, logró pasar a la Q2, dejando fuera a Tsunoda, con todo un RB (con el que su compañero Lindblad fue quinto) y a su compañero en Williams, Alex Albon. Sainz ya sabe lo que es llevarse la pole en Italia, la que logró en 2023 por delante de Leclerc y ha mostrado que con un FW-48 que le daba algunas opciones en recta, le ha sacado todo el rendimiento. Además, su mejor vuelta no fue la del rebufo, algo que no le gusta demasiado, por lo que logró el crono en solitario en el segundo intento de la manga. En la Q2, Carlos superó a Ocon y obtuvo el 15º tiempo, pero con la sanción de Antonelli partirá 14º en la carrera, con opciones de una carrera sólida y de poder buscar los puntos de nuevo. Por su parte, Fernando Alonso superó a Stroll para ser el 21º en tiempos y el 20º en la parrilla, pues Kimi Antonelli deberá salir por detrás por el cambio de unidad de potencia. No pudo luchar con los Cadillac, por esa falta de potencia.

articles.title: Top owner Mike Repole sounds off on issues with horse racing leadership
articles.summary: As one of horse racing's most prominent and successful owners, Mike Repole isn't shy about sharing his opinions and gripes about the sport he loves.
articles.body:
SARATOGA SPRINGS - Mike Repole isn't one to let his soapbox go to waste.

As one of horse racing's most prominent and successful owners, Repole, a 57-year-old Queens native who made his fortune (an estimated $2.5 billion, according to Forbes) in the food and beverage industry, isn't shy about sharing his opinions - especially about the state of the sport he loves.

Because as committed as he is to the sport, Repole - the self-proclaimed "commissioner" of horse racing - has serious concerns about where the thoroughbred game is headed.

He addressed them in an interview with the Times Union at Saratoga Race Course this past Friday, the day before Renegade, whom he co-owns with Robert and Lawana Low, raced to an eighth-place finish in the Travers Stakes .

"If things don't change," Repole said, "I think in 10 years the sport's in serious, serious trouble."

Considering that, when Repole sees an issue he feels needs to be addressed, he's not shy about raising his voice or who his opinions might offend.

"I think that there aren't enough vocal people in this sport," he said, "and I think that there's things that, for some reason, people are afraid to say about the sport."

What Repole, who also serves as a co-owner and director of business operations for the United Football League, wants is for the varying track operators, racing regulators and national organizations to come together in some centralized form, with a figurehead in place to oversee it.

"This is a sport that it's probably the only big sport that doesn't have a commissioner - other than myself, by the way," he said. "I think that if there was more infrastructure and a little bit more of the of the big entities that that affect the sport working together - whether it was NYRA and Churchill (Downs), whether it was the breeding farms, whether it was the Jockey Club, whether it was the bigger owners and the bigger trainers - and really look at the sport in its totality, I think it'd be better."

What Repole isn't a fan of is the Horseracing Integrity and Safety Authority. The organization, empowered by an act of Congress, regulates racing in around two dozen states with a focus on racetrack safety and anti-doping and medication rules.

Repole said that he's "not a fan of government or federal involvement." Horse racing is, in his words, "a very hard sport to police," and HISA "really needs an overhaul and change in order for it to work."

"The safety of the sport should have been a priority for the last 120 years," he said. "Knowing what you know, that you couldn't come up with a solution internally to make the sport safer, cleaner, and better for everyone involved, and most importantly, the horse, that's the shame."

In a statement to the Times Union, a HISA spokesperson said: "We agree (the sport is hard to police), which is exactly why a fragmented, state-by-state regulatory system was not sufficient. HISA was created following a bipartisan act of Congress, signed into law by President Trump, to establish national standards and consistent oversight for a sport that previously operated under a patchwork of different rules and enforcement practices.

"HISA is not static, and we will continue to improve and evolve our programs based on data, science and input from those who work in the sport. But returning to the fragmented system that preceded HISA would not make racing safer, fairer or easier to regulate. The answer to the challenges of regulating this sport is to continue strengthening consistent, nationwide standards - not to abandon them."

Repole's gripes with HISA came into full focus recently with numerous posts on social media criticizing the organization and its handling of a scandal involving Marshall Gramm, an owner and prominent horseplayer. Gramm recently agreed to a provisional suspension banning him from ownership and racetrack activities after he was charged with violating HISA rules for allegedly accessing confidential veterinary treatment records through HISA's informational portal.

Repole isn't the only one raising his voice about HISA. On the same day he spoke with the Times Union, Churchill Downs Incorporated CEO Bill Carstanjen sent a letter to the Federal Trade Commission to "express serious concern" about HISA's "significant questions about the governance, transparency, technology controls, and accountability."

Horse Racing Nation obtained and published the letter, which cited both the recent "Fair Hill Five" betting coup scandal involving races at Saratoga and Monmouth Park, as well as the Gramm controversy, and requested that the FTC initiate an independent review of HISA's handling of the matters.

Among those copied on the letter was U.S. Rep. Paul Tonko, the Amsterdam Democrat and lead sponsor of the legislation that empowered HISA.

HISA isn't the only target of Repole's barbs. The Jockey Club, which has been one of the most powerful organizations in American thoroughbred racing for more than 130 years, is also in his crosshairs.

"To me, it's a failure by the Jockey Club, but more importantly, I think it was to their benefit to put (HISA) on," Repole said. "Remember, they're the ones that pushed for HISA. They're the ones that wrote the bylaws, and they're the ones that still have data with them and share data with them. I think they're as responsible for what's going on as HISA."

In a statement to the Times Union, a spokesperson for The Jockey Club, "The Jockey Club was an early supporter of federal legislation to establish national integrity and safety standards for horse racing," noting that it was one of several entities that had "substantive input into the final bill language," including the Breeders' Cup, Churchill Downs, National Thoroughbred Racing Association, United States Anti-Doping Agency, American Association of Equine Practitioners and Humane Society of the United States.

The statement continued, "Supporting the creation of HISA is not the same as controlling HISA. HISA was deliberately established as an independent organization in accordance with the Horseracing Integrity and Safety Act of 2020 and is responsible for its own operations, regulatory decisions, technology, software, and security. Neither The Jockey Club nor its affiliated companies designed, developed, tested, secured, or maintained the HISA Portal or HISA's internal technology systems. The Jockey Club also has no role in setting, reviewing, or testing HISA's controls over data provided to it."

Along with his problems with the way the sport is overseen, Repole is concerned about the sport's declining foal crop and that smaller breeders, owners and horseplayers may be pushed out of what he perceives as a top-heavy environment.

"I was a small owner before I became a big owner," he said. "I was a small horse player before I became a big horse player, and I think it would be a shame if the game shut them out. And I would be really concerned about the future of the game if the smaller players can't play.

He's concerned that horse racing "had a 100-year head start on gambling, and we wasted it," and that even though he wants a younger generation to become invested in the sport, he's not sure that it's a product ready to be marketed to that audience.

The marketing guru wants to see the sport's internal issues fixed first.

"One of the biggest bonds I have with my daughter is horse racing," Repole said. "She's 11 years old. When she's 51 in 40 years, I want to make sure she takes her kids here. I'm definitely concerned about the future of the sport."
